hub.description: Decks and fences for Shelbyville, TN homes, from lots near the courthouse square to acreage out in Bedford County horse country.
hub.intro: Shelbyville yards come in a lot of shapes. Yours might be a small lot a few blocks from the courthouse square, a newer house on the edge of town that backs up to farmland, or a few acres out in Bedford County with horses next door. Each of those asks something different of a deck or a fence. This page covers what matters first in Shelbyville. For more detail, read about [building a deck in Shelbyville](/deck-builder-shelbyville-tn/) or [fence installation in Shelbyville](/fence-company-shelbyville-tn/).

sections.heading: Town lots and country acreage need different plans
paragraphs: Around Downtown Shelbyville and up North Main, many homes sit on modest lots with neighbors close on both sides. A privacy fence there is mostly about screening the next yard and giving the dog room to run. Decks tend to be low platforms off the back door, sized to fit between the house and the property line. On a lot like that, layout matters more than square footage.

Head out Wartrace Road away from town and lots tend to get larger, with pasture showing up between houses. The questions change out there. Do you fence the whole property, or only the yard around the house? Should the deck face the pasture or the drive? On Shelbyville acreage, a smaller project in the right spot often does more for you than a big one spread thin.

sections.heading: Rock and clay under Shelbyville yards
paragraphs: Much of Bedford County sits on limestone, and in a lot of Shelbyville yards it is not far below the grass. A post hole can go smoothly for a while and then stop on a ledge of rock. Fence posts and deck footings both run into it. Rock is not a reason to skip a project, but the plan should leave room to adjust once digging starts.

Above the rock, many Shelbyville yards have heavy clay. It holds water after a hard rain and shrinks as it dries in late summer. Wood that sits in a wet pocket rots sooner, and footings in soggy ground can shift. Better drainage helps with both. Shaping the soil and the top of each concrete footing so water runs away from the post keeps the wood drier right where rot usually starts.

sections.heading: Lots near the Duck River
paragraphs: The Duck River runs through Shelbyville, and plenty of lots sit close to it or to a creek that drains toward it. Low ground near the water can stay soft for days after a storm, and some of it floods when the river runs high. If your yard has a spot like that, mention it early. It affects where posts can go and how a deck gets framed.

Floodplain rules for Shelbyville lots come from the city or from Bedford County, depending on your address. Before planning a deck or a long fence run on river ground, call the codes office that covers your lot and ask whether any limits apply. Fences need extra thought here too, because a solid run across low ground can hold back water that used to drain through the yard.

sections.heading: Permits, HOAs, and older streets downtown
paragraphs: Inside city limits, permits usually go through the City of Shelbyville. Outside them, ask Bedford County, since county rules are not always the same as the city's. Raised or attached decks often need a permit and inspections. Fence rules are usually lighter, though front yards and corner lots can come with limits. Our [deck permit guide](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) covers the general picture, and the codes office has the final word.

Many established neighborhoods in Shelbyville have no HOA at all. Some newer subdivisions do, and their covenants can spell out fence height and style or where a deck may sit. Get that approval in writing before anything is ordered. If your house is on one of the older streets near the square, ask the city whether any design review applies to your block before you settle on a fence style.

sections.heading: Planning a deck and a fence together
paragraphs: If your Shelbyville project includes both, plan them at the same time. Picture the dog coming down the new deck stairs into a yard that is not fenced yet. When the two are drawn together, the gate lands where people actually walk and the fence does not box in the stairs. Posts for each can also be placed so they do not crowd each other near the house.

Whichever you start with, the first step in Shelbyville is the same. Send your address and a rough idea of the project through the [estimate form](#estimate). Mention anything you already know about the ground, such as rock showing at the surface or a low spot that holds water. Those details shape the plan more than the size of the deck or the length of the fence.

faqs.q: Can one fence keep in my horses and also give my backyard privacy?
faqs.a: Usually not. Horse fencing is built for large animals that lean on it and chew it, and it needs to be easy for them to see. A backyard privacy fence is built to block a view and hold in a dog. On acreage around Shelbyville, it is common to see a pasture fence out in the field and a separate yard fence around the house. Describe the animals and the acreage when you ask for an estimate.

faqs.q: My yard near the creek stays wet. Can a deck or fence still go there?
faqs.a: Often, yes, but the plan has to respect the water. Footings and posts may need to shift toward firmer ground, and a fence may need to stay open where water crosses the yard. If the lot is in a mapped flood zone near the Duck River, check with the City of Shelbyville or Bedford County first. Photos of the yard after a heavy rain tell more than a visit on a dry afternoon.

faqs.q: When should I start planning if I want the project done by summer?
faqs.a: Earlier than most people think. Spring and summer are busy for outdoor work across Middle Tennessee, and permits or HOA approval can add time before any digging starts in Shelbyville. If you plan to host guests during the Tennessee Walking Horse National Celebration in late summer, start the conversation in winter. That leaves room for approvals and weather without a rush at the end.

deck.description: Deck builder in Shelbyville, TN: footings in limestone and clay, raised decks on lots near the Duck River, and freestanding decks for farmhouses.
deck.intro: Building a deck in Shelbyville usually starts below the boards. Limestone sits close to the surface in much of Bedford County. The clay above it holds water, and some yards slope toward the Duck River or a creek that feeds it. A deck that lasts here is one whose footings were planned for that ground. This page walks through what matters on Shelbyville lots, from small yards near downtown to farmhouses on acreage, so you know what to ask any deck builder you talk to.

sections.heading: Sizing a deck for the way you use your Shelbyville yard
paragraphs: Before anyone talks about boards, it helps to know what the deck is for. On a small lot near North Main, it might hold a grill and a couple of chairs, and the real job is fitting it between the back door and the fence line. Out in the county it might be a wide spot to watch the horses at the end of the day. Those are very different decks, and they should be framed and priced differently.

Notice where the afternoon sun lands and which door you walk out of most. If you host family during the Walking Horse Celebration each year, you may want more room for chairs than you use the rest of the summer. A deck that is too big for a narrow yard eats the grass you meant to keep. One that is too small gets outgrown the first time everyone comes over.

sections.heading: Deck footings in Shelbyville limestone and clay
paragraphs: Every deck rests on footings, and in Shelbyville the digging is where surprises show up. A footing hole can hit a shelf of limestone before it reaches the depth on the plan. There are honest ways to handle that. Sometimes the layout shifts a little to find better ground. Other times the rock gets drilled, or the footing is designed to bear on the rock itself. Which one fits depends on the deck and on what the inspector will accept.

Clay causes a different kind of trouble. It holds water after a storm and pulls back from concrete as it dries out. Wood posts left sitting in soggy ground rot faster, even when they are rated for ground contact. A post that stands on a footing above grade, with the soil shaped to drain away, tends to last longer. On a low deck, leave enough open space underneath for air to move, or the framing stays damp.

sections.heading: Raised decks on sloped lots and river ground
paragraphs: A Shelbyville house that sits higher in front than in back, with the yard falling toward a creek or the Duck River, usually calls for a raised deck off the main floor. The far end may stand on tall posts. Those need diagonal bracing so the deck does not sway when people move around on it. Stairs should come down on firm, level ground rather than at the bottom of a wet swale.

Ground close to the river raises its own questions in Shelbyville. Some of it is in a mapped flood zone, and building there can mean extra review from the city or Bedford County. Outside a flood zone, a swale that stays muddy after rain is still a poor place for a footing. If you have watched where water collects in your yard, tell your builder, because that should decide footing placement more than anything on a drawing.

sections.heading: Freestanding decks for farmhouses and older homes
paragraphs: If your home is an older farmhouse out Wartrace Road or elsewhere in Bedford County, attaching a deck takes care. The ledger board that carries one side of an attached deck has to bolt into solid framing. Some older houses do not have that framing where you would expect it. Siding can hide rot, and an old brick or stone foundation may not be a sound place to fasten one.

When the house cannot carry a ledger safely, a freestanding deck is usually the better answer. It stands on its own posts and beams beside the house and does not lean on the old framing at all. Open acreage around Shelbyville brings another concern, which is sun. With no shade trees nearby, decking takes the full heat of the afternoon. Our guide on [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) covers how each material handles Tennessee sun.

sections.heading: Permits and HOA review for a Shelbyville deck
paragraphs: Raised and attached decks often need a permit, and who issues it depends on your address. City residents usually deal with the City of Shelbyville codes office. Outside city limits, check with Bedford County, since its rules do not always match the city's. Inspections commonly happen when the footing holes are dug and again once the framing is up, before boards hide it. The [Tennessee deck permit guide](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains the general process.

In the newer subdivisions around town, read your covenants before anything else. Some HOAs want a drawing and a stain color before they sign off, and a few restrict where on the lot a deck can go. Get approval in writing. Starting before approval is the quickest way to end up tearing out boards you already paid for.

sections.heading: Questions to ask any deck builder in Shelbyville
paragraphs: Whoever you hire, find out how they plan to handle rock if a footing hole hits it, and whether that work is in the price or added later. Ask who pulls the permit and who meets the inspector. Stairs and railing should be spelled out in the bid, along with hauling off an old deck if you have one. A deck builder who answers those plainly is easier to work with. When one bid comes in far below the rest, a missing piece is often the reason.

When you are ready, send your address and a short description through the [estimate form](#estimate). Say whether the deck attaches to the house and how much the yard slopes. Anything you know about rock or wet ground helps too. If you also need a fence, the [Shelbyville fence page](/fence-company-shelbyville-tn/) covers what changes on that side of the job.

faqs.q: Should I repair my old deck or replace it?
faqs.a: It depends on what is failing. Faded or splintered boards are surface wear, and new boards over sound framing can fix that. Soft joists, a ledger pulling away from the house, or posts rotting at the ground line point to structural trouble. In Shelbyville clay, check the posts first, because wet soil at the base is where rot usually starts. Once the structure is failing, a new deck is usually the safer choice.

faqs.q: Does a small ground level deck in Shelbyville need a permit?
faqs.a: Sometimes not, but do not assume. Rules for low decks that stand free of the house can differ between the City of Shelbyville and Bedford County, and codes get updated over time. A short call to the office that covers your address settles it. If you live in an HOA neighborhood, you likely need their approval even when no permit is required, so check with both before you build.

faqs.q: Is a freestanding deck as sturdy as one attached to the house?
faqs.a: It can be, when it is built right. A freestanding deck carries its load on its own posts and beams instead of hanging one side off the house. That means an extra row of posts along the house side and bracing to keep it from racking. On older farmhouses around Shelbyville, it is often the safer choice. It also avoids cutting into siding that may be hiding old damage.

faqs.q: What should I know before adding a deck to a new build in Shelbyville?
faqs.a: Newer lots often have fill dirt that was pushed in during grading, and fill can keep settling for a while. Deck footings need to reach firm native soil rather than stop in loose fill. Watch how the builder graded the yard to drain, since a deck should not block that path. Check your plat for drainage or utility easements along the back line, and get HOA approval before work begins.

faqs.q: Which decking holds up best in Shelbyville humidity?
faqs.a: Under most decks, the framing is pressure treated pine no matter what goes on top. For the surface, pressure treated boards cost less up front but need regular cleaning and a fresh coat of stain or sealer. Composite skips the staining, though it still grows mildew in shade and darker colors get hot in full sun. Decks near the river or under big trees stay damp longer, so plan on washing either kind each spring.

fence.description: Fence company in Shelbyville, TN for privacy fences near downtown, yards that border pasture, rocky post holes, and lots near the Duck River.
fence.intro: Shelbyville fence jobs run from small town lots to open pasture. Near the courthouse square, yards are small and a privacy fence is mostly about screening the neighbors. A few miles out, you see board fence around horse pastures and wire along cattle ground, with newer houses tucked in between. Many of those homeowners need something in the middle, a solid backyard fence that sits next to someone else's farm. This page covers what shapes fence installation in Shelbyville, from rock in the post holes to low ground by the Duck River.

sections.heading: Privacy fences on in town Shelbyville lots
paragraphs: On the older streets around Downtown Shelbyville and North Main, yards tend to be narrow and neighbors are close. A privacy fence there has to work around mature trees and whatever is left of old fence lines. Board on board gives the most screening because the pickets overlap. Shadowbox lets a little air through and looks the same from both sides, which the neighbors tend to like. Our guide to [privacy fence options](/guides/privacy-fence-options/) compares the other styles.

If there is old chain link or wire along your back line, maybe with vines grown through it, removing it has to be planned into the job, and it can take longer than you would guess. Tree roots near the line can push a post off layout, so posts sometimes need to shift a little. Before any digging, Tennessee 811 has to mark buried utilities. On older lots, service lines do not always run in a straight line from the street.

sections.heading: When your Shelbyville yard backs up to pasture
paragraphs: Some newer homes around Shelbyville sit right against working farmland. If your yard borders a neighbor's horses or cattle, that changes how your privacy fence should go in. Horses often chew wood and lean on whatever they can reach. A fence set tight against their pasture fence gives them the chance to do both to yours. Keeping some space between the two fences cuts down on how much of your fence they can get to.

Talk with the neighbor who owns the pasture before you tie into their fence or set posts near it. Their fence may sit on the line or a little off it, and the two of you should agree on who maintains what. If you are not sure where the line runs, a survey usually costs less than moving a fence later. A friendly conversation at the start is easier than an argument after the posts are set.

sections.heading: Setting fence posts in rock and clay
paragraphs: Limestone near the surface is common around Shelbyville and in many parts of Bedford County, and a fence line means digging a lot of holes. The auger may go down clean on one stretch and stop on a shelf of rock a short way down on the next. When that happens, the usual choices are drilling into the rock or adjusting post spacing to land in better spots. Skimping on depth to save time is a bad trade, because shallow posts tend to lean after a wet winter.

In Shelbyville yards, the clay around the post matters as much as the rock under it. It holds water, and wood that stays wet at the ground line rots first. Concrete around each post should be crowned at the top so rain runs off instead of collecting against the wood. Posts rated for ground contact hold up much longer than lumber meant for above ground use. That is why cedar pickets on pressure treated posts are a common pairing.

sections.heading: Fencing low ground near the Duck River
paragraphs: If your Shelbyville yard dips toward the Duck River or one of the creeks that feed it, think hard before running a solid fence across the low spot. A privacy fence there acts like a small dam. When water rises, it catches leaves and limbs, and the pressure can push a section over. It can also send runoff toward a neighbor's lot, which is a hard problem to fix once the fence is up.

Across a drainage path, it often works better to leave a gap at the bottom or switch to an open style for that stretch. Sometimes the right move is stopping short and using a gate. If your lot is in a mapped flood zone, ask the city or Bedford County what is allowed before planning the run. Posts in soft river ground may need extra depth or a wider footing to stay plumb.

sections.heading: Fencing a dog yard on a bigger lot
paragraphs: On acreage out Wartrace Road and elsewhere around Shelbyville, fencing the whole property just for a dog often makes little sense. A fenced yard around the house, with a gate toward the barn or the drive, keeps the dog close and takes far less material than a perimeter run. Think about how your dog gets out. Diggers need the bottom closed, and climbers need a solid face without easy footholds. Our guide on the [best fence for dogs](/guides/best-fence-for-dogs/) goes through each habit.

Gates see more use than any other part of a fence, so put them where you really walk and drive the mower. A gate too narrow for the mower tends to get propped open, and then it keeps nothing in. Self closing hinges and a latch that catches on its own help with kids and delivery drivers. Gate posts carry the most load on the line, so they usually get deeper holes and more concrete than line posts.

sections.heading: Surveys, permits, and HOA rules for a Shelbyville fence
paragraphs: Property lines around Shelbyville can be hard to read, especially on rural land. Older deeds sometimes describe a boundary by a creek or an old fence, and both can change over the years. On town lots, the corner pins may be buried or missing. Either way, the line needs to be settled before fence installation starts. Our guide to [fences and property lines](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) explains why the survey comes first.

Permit rules for fences can differ between the City of Shelbyville and Bedford County, so call the codes office that covers your address. If you live in a subdivision with an HOA, get written approval on height and style before materials are ordered. Once those answers are in hand, send your address and a short note through the [estimate form](#estimate). Tell us what the fence needs to keep in and what it needs to hide.

faqs.q: Will a privacy fence hold up next to my neighbor's horses?
faqs.a: It can, with some planning. Set your fence back from the pasture fence rather than sharing a line with it, so the horses cannot reach your boards over their own fence. If the pasture fence is in poor shape, talk to the owner first, because a loose horse leaning on your fence is trouble for both of you. Heavier posts and rails on the pasture side help, and so does agreeing on who keeps up the strip between the two fences.

faqs.q: Can I put a fence in my front yard in Shelbyville?
faqs.a: Often, but front yards are where local rules tend to bite. Limits on height and style commonly apply near the street and around corners where drivers need to see. The City of Shelbyville and Bedford County may handle this differently, and an HOA may add its own rules on top. Check with the codes office and your HOA before you pick a style or order anything.

faqs.q: Will a privacy fence keep deer out of my garden?
faqs.a: It can help. Deer are less likely to jump into a space they cannot see into, so a solid fence works differently than an open one of the same height. A short open fence will not stop a determined deer. On a rural Shelbyville lot, fencing just the garden with a tall solid fence is often more practical than trying to fence the whole property.

faqs.q: Does rock in my yard make fence installation cost more?
faqs.a: It can. Drilling through limestone takes more time and different tools than digging through clay, so a line full of rock usually costs more than one without. Nobody knows exactly until the holes are dug. That is why it helps to ask how rock is priced before you sign, so it does not show up later as a surprise on the bill.

faqs.q: What should I ask a fence company before hiring them?
faqs.a: Start with how they handle rock in the post holes and whether that is priced in or billed later. Find out who calls Tennessee 811 and who handles a permit if one is needed. The layout and gate locations should be in writing. A fence company that answers plainly on those points will be easier to deal with when something unexpected turns up in Shelbyville ground.
